Former Countdown host and Australian music champion Molly Meldrum, who has died aged 83. Photograph: Martin Philbey/WireImage

Tributes flow for Molly Meldrum: Human Nature, Jason Donovan and others remember music industry great

Peter Andre, Richard Wilkins and Kate Ceberano share memories of ‘a truly unique character’ and ‘the fan all artists wish to have’

• Molly Meldrum, Countdown host and promoter of Australian music, dies aged 83

• Molly Meldrum – a life in pictures

• Ian ‘Molly’ Meldrum – obituary

Friends and fans of Molly Meldrum have remembered the music industry great, who died on Monday at the age of 83.

Meldrum spent more than a decade hosting the ABC music show Countdown, leaving a lasting legacy on the Australian music landscape.

Jason Donovan said Meldrum was the “very heart” of the music program while he was growing up, calling the man a “truly unique character, a great Australian and one of this country’s greatest pioneers and ambassadors for music and entertainment”.

Molly Meldrum, Countdown host and promoter of Australian music, dies aged 83

Read more

“He was loved, recognised and respected around the world for the extraordinary contribution he made to Australian music and the artists he championed,” Donovan wrote on Facebook. “There will never be another quite like him.”

The former Neighbours star shared a memory of Meldrum appearing on an episode alongside Kylie Minogue and Guy Pearce, adding: “What a day that was!”

The television presenter Richard Wilkins remembered his longtime friend on-air on Monday morning. The pair used to travel around the world for interviews, Wilkins said, which led to great memories and hilarious stories.

“Australian music would not be Australian music without Molly’s incredible contribution,” Wilkins said. “I shared so many overseas trips with Molly, which was a joy and a curse. He lost 13 passports, that was the tally I got to.

“We went from a Michael Jackson gig in Munich to see Bruce Springsteen in Paris. That was the sort of thing we used to get up to back in the day.”

Gavin Wood, a longtime friend of Meldrum’s who worked on Countdown, said the host was “one of the craziest, most colourful, funniest and most beautiful people you could ever have the pleasure of meeting”.

“What he has done for the Australian music industry is simply phenomenal,” Wood wrote. “His contribution, passion, enthusiasm and unwavering commitment to Australian artists helped shape an entire generation of music and entertainment.

“There will never be another Molly Meldrum. You simply cannot measure anyone against him.”

Meldrum with Kylie Minogue at the 1989 Aria awards. Meldrum featured in an episode of Neighbours alongside Minogue and Guy Pearce. Photograph: Patrick Riviere/Getty Images

Bands and artists echoed those sentiments.

“He was such a huge presence in the Australian music industry and was a great friend and supporter of so many up and coming bands and artists – ourselves included,” the band Human Nature wrote. “Thanks for everything Molly. Rest easy.”

The singer Peter Andre posted a photo with Meldrum, praising him for helping to elevate his career and saying “this really hurts”.

“If it wasn’t for this man, I would not of had any of the chances I had to make it in any way in the entertainment industry back when it was near impossible to get noticed,” Andre wrote. “He believed in me from day one and I am forever grateful to Ian ‘Molly’ Meldrum.”

Ian ‘Molly’ Meldrum: chaotic but inspirational champion of Australian music – obituary

Read more

Kate Ceberano wrote: “He had no agenda he wanted, no praise, he never basked in any reflected glory or self pride. He simply wanted the world to hear what he could hear, wanted you to see what he was looking at and then blow it up to 11. Way up sky high. No dream is too big. No cringe, withholding nothing.

“He was the fan all artists wish to have.”

The Australian Recording Industry Association issued its own praise of Meldrum’s work, noting that both he and the Countdown program were the first inductees into the Aria Hall of Fame who weren’t recording artists, back in 2014.

“It is impossible to imagine what Australian music would look like without Molly’s long and storied career,” said Annabelle Herd, Aria’s chief executive. “He shaped the music taste of a generation of Australians and gave so much of himself for the good of Australian artists, for which our whole industry is eternally grateful.”

The St Kilda football club remembered Meldrum as a “lifelong Sainter”, saying the organisation was deeply saddened by his death.

“An iconic and passionate supporter of our football club, Molly changed and brightened the lives of so many across a storied career,” the club wrote on Facebook.

items.title: 'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes
items.summary: The BBC's Sarah Rainsford reports from the scene of a collapsed residential building in Ukraine's Kyiv region.
items.body:
'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes

'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes

At least three bodies have been recovered the site of a residential building that was hit by a Russian strike in the Kyiv region, Ukraine's State Emergency Services said.

A woman in her forties and a teenage boy have so far been identified as rescue workers continue to search the rubble for those who are still trapped.

Continued warnings of further drone threats near the site are hampering efforts, the service added, but some people were successfully evacuated earlier in the day.

"We are living a nightmare... only God knows when it will end," one woman told the BBC's Sarah Rainsford, who's reporting from Ukraine's Kyiv region.

Molly Meldrum, Countdown host and promoter of Australian music, dies aged 83

Much-loved broadcaster played a critical role in exposing rest of the world to Australian music – and vice versa

• Ian ‘Molly’ Meldrum – obituary

Molly Meldrum, the Australian music journalist, broadcaster and producer, has died at the age of 83.

He died peacefully in the early hours of Monday morning at a hospital in Melbourne, his longtime friend and manager Mark Klemens confirmed to the Guardian.

“We have lost a true Australian icon, a man who opened doors for so many and entertained millions of people here and around the world,” Klemens said. “He was unconventional and wonderfully unpredictable, but always caring, always funny and always down to earth, with a passion the rest of us could only envy. He made the most of his life, and boy, was it a full one. Rest in peace, Molly.”

“Affectionately dubbed ‘the Guru’, Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music. He shaped not only the sound of a nation but also the dreams of generations who grew up with his voice guiding them,” his partner Yan Wongngam and family said in a statement, issued by Klemens.

“Yan cared for Molly with great love and devotion, especially through his final years. The family is deeply grateful to him, to Molly’s many loyal friends, and to the staff at Epworth Richmond for their wonderful care.”

Ian ‘Molly’ Meldrum: chaotic but inspirational champion of Australian music – obituary

Read more

The Stetson-wearing Countdown presenter is credited with engineering the breakthrough of Abba, Blondie and Madonna in Australia. During his time on the wildly popular Sunday evening ABC music show from 1974 to 1987, he championed songs including Blondie’s In the Flesh, John Mellencamp’s I Need a Lover, Duran Duran’s Planet Earth and Madonna’s Holiday, transforming then unknown tracks into Top 10 hits in Australia.

Meldrum also passionately promoted Australian performers, giving exposure on Countdown to dozens who went on to local or international fame, including INXS, Kylie Minogue, Skyhooks and Mental as Anything.

Meldrum never disguised his unabashed fervour as a fan, even while forming decades-long friendships with an array of global stars.

He developed an obsession with the Beatles after their explosion on to the world stage, and eventually interviewed his pop idol, John Lennon, who fed him the scoop of the band’s impending break-up. But Meldrum did nothing with the incendiary information because he “was so in awe” of Lennon.

Born Ian Meldrum in Orbost, Victoria, to a family he called “quite dysfunctional”, the larger-than-life character moved to live with an aunt and uncle in Shepparton from the age of 12. He went from wanting to be a conductor to becoming entranced with the idea of producing music and later lived with the family of his close friend, the singer Ronnie Burns.

He was one of the first openly gay personalities on Australian television and was known for his bumbling interview technique and for his chaotic and colourful scuffles. On the 40th anniversary of Countdown in 2014, Prince Charles recalled a shambolic 1977 interview with Meldrum, telling the ABC: “There is an old show business saying which warns never to work with animals or children, but nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum.”

Countdown at 50: the powerful, messy and sexy music show that changed Australia

Read more

Meldrum began appearing on camera on Countdown in mid-1975, delivering the weekly Rock Report, redubbed Humdrum by a guest host, John Paul Young. While reviewing albums, Meldrum would often hold LPs up awkwardly, making them hard to see under the glare of stage lights. ABC policy prohibited hosts endorsing products, so “do yourself a favour” became Meldrum’s catchphrase.

In the 1980s Meldrum landed various presenting gigs on television: the 1985 Oz for Africa concert, the Australian leg of Live Aid; the ABC interview show The Meldrum Tapes and a regular music segment, Molly’s Melodrama, on the variety show Hey Hey It’s Saturday.

In 2011 Meldrum fell from a ladder in the back yard of his Melbourne home and was placed in intensive care in a critical condition, undergoing surgery for head and spinal injuries. After four months he recovered enough to begin appearing in public again.

In 1986 he was made a member of the Order of Australia, with a citation for “service to the fostering of international relief and to youth”. In 2012 he was inducted into the Logie Hall of Fame. In 2014, when Meldrum became the first non-recording artist to be inducted into the Aria Hall of Fame, Minogue said the Australian music industry was “blessed to have had you in our lives for over four decades”.

Elton John was similarly unreserved in his praise, saying in 2019: “I don’t think anyone has done more for music in Australia than Molly Meldrum.”

Meldrum is survived by his partner, Yan Wongngam, his adopted son and his two younger brothers.

items.body:
Abdul El-Sayed speaks about the Democrats’ historic midterm success and his priorities as a senator during the Atlantic’s summit in Washington DC on 17 November. Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters

Abdul El-Sayed speaks about the Democrats’ historic midterm success and his priorities as a senator during the Atlantic’s summit in Washington DC on 17 November. Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters

Abdul El-Sayed doubles down on ‘TrumpCare’ health plan, urging president to ‘get it done’

Democratic senator-elect reiterates suggestion to rename Medicare for All after Trump if president allows bill to pass

Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage.

“If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.”

El-Sayed made those remarks on Sunday on NBC’s Meet the Press, where he reiterated his pledge to pursue a single-payer, national healthcare program after the Democrat became the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate during the midterms earlier in November.

‘I agree with the president’: incoming senator Abdul El-Sayed seeks to help Trump end military aid to Israel

Read more

Trump’s Republican party is going to lose control of Congress for the second half of his second presidency. But the president has made clear his intention to wield his legislative veto powers whenever he sees fit.

Appearing on Sunday’s Meet the Press, El-Sayed said he would not mind Medicare for All – a big part of his campaign platform – being named “TrumpCare” as long as such a program came into existence.

“I care that the people of this country finally have the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country. And if the president is serious about leaving a lasting legacy, there is nothing better than the ultimate Trump card,” El-Sayed said to Meet the Press host Kristen Welker, making a double entendre for a term that – when the T is lowercase – also refers to a card that beats out others in card games.

El-Sayed told Welker that such a Trump card would be in effect “from the moment [people] are born to the moment that they pass away – that guarantees them the healthcare that has been so elusive in this country without premiums, co-pays and deductibles”.

The senator-elect’s comments come after he previously suggested to CNN that he is not above stroking Trump’s prodigious ego to get legislation passed – including by naming Medicare for All “TrumpCare”.

He also previously wrote on social media, alongside images of a gold health insurance card with “TrumpCare” inscribed on it: “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

Trump has spent much of his second presidency trying to get as much as possible named after him – from institutions, physical buildings and currency.

El-Sayed also said that he supports healthcare reform proposed by Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator.

‘A complete repudiation’: public health won big in US midterm elections

Read more

Sanders’ proposal would create a single-payer system in which the federal government insures everybody, financed by an increase in taxes, while eliminating private insurance.

But El-Sayed said he is not focused on eliminating private insurance as an option, which Sanders aims to eliminate by having everything primary and preventive services to hospital stays covered under his proposed plan. Out-of-pocket costs on deductibles and co-pays – staples of the rapacious private insurance industry to which most Americans must resort – would also be eliminated under Sanders’ plan.

El-Sayed said he wants to “provide you basic public health insurance no matter who you are in this country” while being open to the idea of not taking alternative options away.

The senator-elect said he has a meeting on the books with JD Vance. El-Sayed would not share the agenda of the meeting, but he confirmed that the vice-president’s chief of staff contacted him after his election victory.

Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking they had woken up in around 2018 – and not being especially pleased at the idea.

For Tory MPs and activists with a full set of Brexit campaign medals, this risks being especially triggering. May’s repeated attempts to cobble together a departure deal that could unite her party involved repeated humiliations, among them the heaviest ever parliamentary defeat for a British PM, when the Commons rejected her Brexit plan by a majority of 230.

With the afterglow of Boris Johnson’s “get Brexit done” 2019 election triumph now seven years and four prime ministers ago, under Kemi Badenoch the party has opted to do less of the, in David Cameron’s resonant phrase, “banging on about Europe” and instead focus on policy areas such as the economy, social security and defence.

The reasons for this caution are obvious. To begin with, even more ardent Tory Brexiters struggle to articulate any tangible benefits to the UK in the decade since the referendum, beyond slightly niche constitutional points about self-determination.

In her BBC interview, May, who comments sparingly on live political subjects despite being an active Tory peer, did not even try to argue that Brexit had been a success, instead saying it was impossible to know, given events such as Covid and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and then adding: “I don’t think Britain’s state today is about whether or not we left the European Union.”

Many voters are much clearer about what they think. Polling suggests that a clear majority of Britons view Brexit as both a failure and a mistake in the first place, with similar support for rejoining the EU, although this depends in part on the pre-conditions for doing so.

This is a product of both lived experience and what pollsters delicately call “demographic churn” – that is, the death of many of the disproportionately older Britons who voted leave and their replacement on the electoral rolls by younger people with more positive views about the EU.

items.body:
The Cop31 president of negotiations and Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, Chris Bowen (centre), looks on before the plenary session at the UN climate change conference in Antalya, Turkey on Sunday. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters

The Cop31 president of negotiations and Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, Chris Bowen (centre), looks on before the plenary session at the UN climate change conference in Antalya, Turkey on Sunday. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters

Analysis

Cop31 left Chris Bowen stuck between petrostates and climate reality. But the failure to say the f-word is not his alone

Graham Readfearn in Antalya

Australia’s climate change minister will face a torrent of criticism over his role, but disagreement over fossil fuels proved an unbridgeable sticking point

After delivering a major speech to the UN climate talks in Turkey last week, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, dismissed criticisms that he hadn’t managed to name the problem that is overwhelming driving catastrophic global heating – burning fossil fuels.

“You could pick out any number of things that were not in what was a short speech,” he later said.

If Albanese really thought the head of a leading coal and gas exporter failing to address the issue head-on was inconsequential or trivial, then his climate change minister, Chris Bowen, will have a story for him after the finals days of the fractious talks that became the longest UN climate summit ever.

Cop31 failed but in ‘the real world’ the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable

Read more

Those talks failed spectacularly to nail its prime ambition – an “Antalya pact” that was meant to drive investment in renewable energy and electrification, boost finance to help developing countries facing worsening climate damage, and acknowledge the world is bursting through a goal of limiting the increase in global temperatures to 1.5C, with alarming consequences across the planet.

As president of negotiations, Bowen barely slept for three days, and on the final night caught only a few moments of shut-eye on a couch in the office where a parade of negotiators had been coming to sit and talk to him.

Many of them raised a “red line” they said was non-negotiable – that any agreement from the summit must refer to the need for the world to “transition away from fossil fuels” that had previously been agreed at talks in Dubai three years ago. Others, including Saudi Arabia, didn’t want the words “fossil fuels” mentioned at all.

A compromise was proposed in the two final drafts of what was meant to be a “cover decision” – an overarching agreement that all countries would back. Drawn up by Bowen and his verbose Turkish counterpart, Cop31 president Murat Kurum, it suggested countries would “recall” the decision in Dubai “in its entirety” – effectively acknowledge its existence – but not say fossil fuels directly.

The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, Norway and Belize were among the countries that said no. Ireland’s climate minister, Darragh O’Brien, said the omission was “unconscionable” and the EU could not support it. Climate campaigners agreed.

Bowen, takes questions from the media in Antalya, Turkey on Sunday. Photograph: Osmancan Gurdogan/Anadolu/Getty Images

With the scheduled Friday finish of the summit a distant memory, Bowen left the stage of the plenary hall late on Sunday afternoon when it was clear too many countries could not accept the text that he had helped put on the table.

Speaking to journalists, Bowen said “Australia left nothing on the field” but the red lines he and his staff tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”. In particular, the way a transition away from fossil fuels was mentioned.

Some countries said they couldn’t support a pact that didn’t mention it, and others “insisted if it was mentioned, they would veto”. “I would have been happy with transition away from fossil fuels being in the text, but that was not going to get support,” Bowen said.

Bowen said despite the breakdown, “in the real world” the transition away from fossil fuels was inevitable and irreversible – and happening at speed. A promised electrification target – that 35% of final energy will come from electricity by 2035, a step that analysis has found could significantly cut fossil fuel use – had the backing of more than 90 countries and was not a deal-breaker.

The climate minister will be presented with a torrent of criticism that the talks failed and he failed. Much domestic news coverage has focused on the cost of Cop31 to Australian taxpayers, rather than the substantive issues being dealt with.

In Antalya, the narrative out of the talks was quite different. Some said the rejection of the pact was a line in the sand that showed the world was no longer willing to accept lukewarm responses on the climate crisis that bent to the whims of fossil fuel interests and petrostates. Some nations are setting up voluntary pacts outside the UN negotiations to try to get the results they need.

Despite some claims in the dramatic final hours, the talks did not actually collapse. Many less controversial elements of the convention’s myriad processes were passed.

But the talks did fail to agree to the Antalya pact that Bowen and Kurum had spent so much political capital on. Some of this failure may be down to the Cop process itself – its reliance on consensus to pass agreements creates plenty of opportunities for countries to block and delay.

Luke Menzel, the chief executive of the Energy Efficiency Council, a membership group focused on electrification in Australia, was at the talks for the full two weeks. He says the reality is “this process has been fracturing for a long time” and had become much tougher after years of wars, rising geopolitical tension and a fuel price crisis caused by conflict in Iran.

“It turns out Antalya is where the conference finally fractured. In many ways it is remarkable we have had as many Cops as we have had in a row that have achieved a consensus,” he says.

Finance, fossil fuels and the ‘overshoot’: six key takeaways from Cop31

Read more

Many climate experts and high-profile figures were left questioning whether the Cop process needs major revision. The former US vice-president and long-time climate campaigner Al Gore was among them, arguing it was “an outrage” that “a handful of petrostates have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels” and concluding “it has been clear for years that the Cop process is in need of significant reform”.

Some campaigners sharply criticised Australia’s role. Denise Cauchi, the chief executive of Climate Action Network Australia, said it had “failed to broker an agreement” and “caved” to the hundreds of lobbyists that were pushing for controversial carbon capture and storage technology to be promoted in the pact. Its attempted inclusion was seen as a sop to fossil fuel interests.

But some from Pacific nations, who see the breach of the 1.5C temperature goal as existential and whose interests Bowen had promised to champion, said the failure in Antalya is shared more widely.

In the chaotic final plenary session, the Fijian climate change minister, Lynda Tabuya, addressed Bowen directly as the rest of the world listened.

“You have tried your utmost best, and we have seen it. Your door has always been open,” she said. “This work is hard – sleepless nights, and over hours and days of constant negotiations. This is not easy but we do it and we do it for our people.

“The failure here is not yours to carry. It is the responsibility of all parties.”

items.title: Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack
items.summary: No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the s…
items.body:
Smoke rises from a fire after an explosion on Merkury, a Russian warship docked at Benghazi port, Libya. Photograph: 2026 Planet Labs PBC/Reuters

Smoke rises from a fire after an explosion on Merkury, a Russian warship docked at Benghazi port, Libya. Photograph: 2026 Planet Labs PBC/Reuters

Blast on Russian ship in Benghazi a suspected drone attack, say Libyan authorities

No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia

An explosion on a Russian ship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya’s eastern-based government has said.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the suspected strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range barrages against Russia far beyond the frontlines.

“Initial investigations indicate that the explosion occurred onboard a Russian ship docked in the port,” said the administration backed by the military commander Khalifa Haftar. “It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones.”

Authorities in divided Libya’s east said the vessel had stopped at Benghazi port to refuel and ⁠resupply on its way back to Russia, ​under maritime cooperation agreements between ‌the two ‌countries.

Two medical sources said no deaths had been ‌reported from the blast, but there were injuries. The number and nationalities of those injured are not yet known.

There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack.

An explosion on the ship in Benghazi, where it had been refuelling on its way back to Russia. Photograph: X.com

The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.

It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible.

“The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the five-year war.

But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians in another continent and the working of the port.

A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.

Initial reports and footage suggest the ship was struck from above, potentially by a drone, launched no more than a few kilometres away from the target in port.

Russia is close to the Benghazi authorities that control eastern Libya. It uses the port to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean, which has a growing importance after it lost bases in Syria.

Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

Emergency services are working to extinguish a fire onboard the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, which was struck in the Baltic Sea. Photograph: Finnish Border Guard/Reuters

The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.

On Sunday visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.

Pictures ​and video released earlier by the Finnish coastguard showed several ‌vessels spraying the Sparta II with ‌water cannons during the night in an attempt to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.

“Smoke is still coming from the vessel, and ​there is clearly still heat onboard,” said Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, a sea safety officer and commander of the maritime sub-centre Helsinki for the Finnish border guard, at a press conference on Sunday.

Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.

The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

items.title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
items.summary: The couple have been together for four years and were engaged in 2025.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByHenry Moore

Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.

Photos of the wedding on Saturday show the ceremony took place by a swimming pool with the pair standing under an arch covered in white flowers.

The singer's mother, Tish Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, were in attendance, Entertainment Tonight reported.

Clayton made t…
items.body:
Director of national intelligence Jay Clayton testifies during a House committee on Homeland Security hearing on Capitol Hill on 18 November 2026. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Director of national intelligence Jay Clayton testifies during a House committee on Homeland Security hearing on Capitol Hill on 18 November 2026. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

US intelligence chief says he trusts Trump’s description of Putin as ‘my friend’

Jay Clayton was pressed on Trump’s characterization of Putin during media appearances on Sunday

Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Donald Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China.

Friend zone: rejected by US voters, Trump enjoys autocrats’ warm embrace

Read more

Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. After a backlash at home and aboard, Trump doubled down on Saturday and posted a photo of himself and Putin shaking hands with the caption “My Friend.”

On CNN’s State of the Union, Dana Bash asked Clayton whether he also thinks Putin is a friend to the US.

“The president is the greatest conductor of foreign policy in a very challenging time that we have seen,” said Clayton on Sunday. “Getting the three nuclear powers together and getting them to agree that they are not going to escalate, that they are going to communicate, that is historic. That is remarkable and, in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely.”

'It's my friend!': Trump hails 'great relationship' with Putin at Apec summit – video

Bash pressed on whether Clayton personally agrees that Putin should be considered a friend.

“Dana, in different contexts, you can use different words. The president pulling off that summit, getting the three of them together, is just remarkable,” Clayton replied.

Speaking with ABC’s Jonathan Karl on This Week, Clayton made similar comments, saying that “using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate” in the context of the summit.

“That conversation, that picture – historic, historic picture – was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers, getting together and saying, ‘We cannot have a nuclear incident,’” Clayton said on Sunday, referring to Trump’s post. “In that circle of that conversation, using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate.”

Clayton also dodged when asked again whether he thinks Putin should be considered a friend to the United States.

“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton responded.

Last week, Trump sidestepped questions about his views on a friendship with Putin.

“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said in a press briefing. “I have fantastic relationships with Putin, that’s a very good thing.”

Trump’s characterization of Putin has sparked backlash from US lawmakers and officials abroad.

“Who is he? He’s the man who has abducted tens of thousands of children, killed tens of thousands of civilians, targeted civilian infrastructure across Ukraine, detained Americans wrongfully, and continues to do so daily,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media.

“Embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” Schumer added. “Senate Democrats will always stand with Ukraine and against Putin and autocratic dictators around the world.”

“It’s beyond me,” Senator Jeanne Shaheen said in an interview with MS NOW. “I don’t understand the president’s admiration and cozying up to Vladimir Putin, who is a war criminal.”

Trump’s comments also drew rebukes abroad, including from the deputy leader of the rightwing party Reform UK.

“It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake,” Richard Tice told Sky News. “He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”

Trump’s description of ​Putin as a friend also drew criticism from European ​allies of Ukraine. “Mr ‌Putin is ​not our ​friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said.

Separately, Clayton also faced questions about the recent spate of technology outages across the US and said Americans should expect more disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems.

“And ​as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, ⁠interruptions in service,” Clayton said on CNN’s State of the Union program. “That is ⁠going to happen.”

• Associated Press contributed reporting

items.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
items.summary: Libya's eastern government says the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia.
items.body:
Image source, Planet Labs PBC

Image caption,

Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire early on Sunday morning

ByHafsa Khalil

Updated 4 minutes ago

An explosion has occurred on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port after a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.

It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS said the country was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Seperately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".

Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.

items.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
items.summary: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.
items.body:
Image source, Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images

Image caption,

Chuck Hubbard is a former journalist whose first political campaign was in 2022

ByMadeline Halpert

The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.

The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.

The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.

Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

• View the 2026 midterm election results

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."

Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images

Image caption,

Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives

Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.

Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.

President Donald Trump himself has suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses, as well as Vice President JD Vance.

Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.

However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

items.summary: John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang ’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most ex…
items.body:
Jensen Huang attends a media roundtable meeting in Singapore in December 2023. Photograph: Edgar Su/Reuters

Jensen Huang attends a media roundtable meeting in Singapore in December 2023. Photograph: Edgar Su/Reuters

Jensen Huang’s reported affair was ‘most expensive sex since Helen of Troy’, US senator says

John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips

Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.

Howard Lutnick has been Trump’s ally for decades. His ties to Nvidia may spell his downfall

Read more

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, where the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.

On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union, the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.

“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.

Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.

Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders are either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.

He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.

John Kennedy speaks to the media on 10 November, the day of the Senate Republican caucus leadership elections at the US Capitol in Washington DC. Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters

“And if secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.

Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.

“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.

A former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, Kennedy delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.

Many believe Kennedy resorts to the drawl to come off as folksy – while he holds degrees from Vanderbilt University, the University of Virginia School of Law and the UK’s Oxford University, and is estimated to be one of the wealthiest US senators.

items.body:
House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries at a news conference at the Capitol on 12 November 2026. Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries at a news conference at the Capitol on 12 November 2026. Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

Democrats capture at least 258 House seats in largest sweep since 1992

Milestone reached Sunday, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Virginia Foxx in North Carolina

House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in a midterm election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Public diaries show the Queensland premier David Crisafulli, pictured, has met with datacentre executives 13 times in the past three years. Photograph: Darren England/AAP

Public diaries show the Queensland premier David Crisafulli, pictured, has met with datacentre executives 13 times in the past three years. Photograph: Darren England/AAP

Datacentre bosses met Australian state premiers and ministers almost 120 times in three years, analysis finds

Transparency International says Queensland’s David Crisafulli was ‘by far the most frequently accessed’ state leader, with 13 meetings

• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Bosses at 10 datacentre companies secured almost 120 meetings with premiers and ministers in five states over a three-year period, with experts declaring this is “just the tip of the iceberg”.

Analysis by Transparency International Australia argues these meetings, when combined with political donations, demonstrates “unfettered access” to decision makers that creates an “uneven playing field”.

The report found donations from major datacentre companies and their contracted lobbying firms nearly tripled over the last three years from $685,000 to $1.8m, coinciding with increased investment across Australia.

The analysis found the Queensland leader, David Crisafulli, was “by far the most frequently accessed state premier”, public diaries showing he has met datacentre executives 13 times in the past three years.

This included three meetings in as many weeks in August and September with Australia’s largest datacentre operator, NextDC, roughly one month before the company’s expansion in Melbourne was halted after its power provider delayed construction of new power poles due to community backlash.

“Those meetings took place shortly before the Queensland premier announced a dedicated framework to fast-track datacentre approvals by taking them out of the hands of local councils,” the Transparency International report said.

Crisafulli has embraced datacentre investment and flew to the United States in September to secure a $31.9bn deal with the AI giant Anthropic for what could become Australia’s largest datacentre. His office was contacted for comment.

‘Communities are really angry’: how Australia’s datacentre opposition has gone from marginal to mainstream in five months

Read more

During this three-year period, 119 meetings with ministers or premiers were held in New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, Queensland and the ACT. These are the only jurisdictions to publicly release ministerial diaries. The meetings were mostly held in 2026.

“These numbers are just the tip of the iceberg.” said Clancy Moore, the chief executive of Transparency International Australia.

“What we don’t know is how many meetings companies like NextDC, OpenAI and Anthropic and their third party lobbyists are having with the prime minister and ministers in our federal parliament.

“Australia’s lobbying laws also don’t cover in-house lobbyists or government relations staff so there’s very little oversight of their activities too.”

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

The report also found Australian company Firmus Technologies secured 10 meetings with Tasmanian ministers and the premier this year alone. During this period, the company’s expansion in the state has faced sustained backlash from local communities who feel they were not properly consulted.

The three companies that secured the most meetings with ministers were Amazon Web Services, Macquarie Technology Group and NextDC.

Last month, Guardian Australia reported on political donations from Amazon and Macquarie to both major parties, closely aligning with the announcement of multi-million dollar government contracts or planning developments. Both companies say these donations were not aimed at influencing policy and that their timing was coincidental.

A shareholder at NextDC’s annual general meeting on Friday said the company had “a lot of lobbying going on in Canberra” but called on the company to better lobby the public on the benefits of datacentres.

The company’s chair, Stephen Flynn, said he was “not sure we are great at lobbying as an industry or as a company” but the world had now changed.

“We thought we were just going along and [being] invisible, in the way if you think about all telecommunications systems … [it] is kind of invisible. We just take it for granted. But we can’t do that. We can’t do that as we go forward.”

The report has also cited examples of four senior public servants at federal government departments quitting to assume leadership positions at OpenAI, AirTrunk and CDC. Three of these appointments were made this year.

In September, the president of the Australian Professional Government Relations Association, Sally Mackenzie, said the scale of engagement between industry and ministers was a sign of the system working as intended.

“What we’re seeing with AI and datacentres is that dynamic playing out at real pace, because the stakes for industry, government and Australians more broadly are so high,” Mackenzie said.

“Lobbying is an important part of the democratic process. It ensures that all stakeholders have the ability to communicate with government.”

items.body:
What's next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?

What's next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?

The COP31 climate summit in Turkey has officially come to an end after countries failed to come to a consensus on a new deal.

The European Union and some other countries rejected a fourth draft agreement over its failure to mention a need to phase out fossil fuels, the largest driver of global climate change.

An EU representative accuses some oil states of hijacking talks, as Russia defends opposing the inclusion of such a commitment and levels direct criticism at the EU in its speech.

The talks have been the longest-running in the summit's history, with negotiations breaking down two days after they had been due to end.

BBC climate and science reporter Esme Stallard reports from Antalya, in Turkey.

items.summary: Exclusive: Thirty-one trusts issue stark warning that cost-cutting demands threaten their ability to function normally Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian ca…
items.body:
Six of the trusts have given lack of money a rating of 25 – the highest possible score – in their risk register. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA

Six of the trusts have given lack of money a rating of 25 – the highest possible score – in their risk register. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA

NHS savings drive leaves hospitals in England facing ‘unpalatable’ cuts

Exclusive: Thirty-one trusts issue stark warning that cost-cutting demands threaten their ability to function normally

Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

Thirty-one health service trusts in England have issued stark warnings that NHS demands for them to make huge budget savings this year threaten their ability to function normally. All have declared that as a threat in the register of risks they have to maintain and publish.

Twenty-seven of those trusts are in such dire financial straits that they have rated lack of money as the biggest threat they face. Six have given that danger a rating of 25 – the highest possible score – in their risk register. A much-larger number of trusts have launched cost-cutting programmes to save as much as £106m each this year by limiting the services they provide and shrinking their workforces, despite understaffing being widespread across the NHS.

The six include King’s College hospital NHS trust in London, which is seeking to save £85m this year, and the St George’s, Epsom and St Helier hospital group, also in the capital, which has a savings target of £91m. The others are the North Midlands, Gloucestershire, and Doncaster and Bassetlaw acute trusts, and Birmingham and Solihull mental health trust.

Trust bosses say their finances are in a “precarious” and “severe” state. They blame rising drug prices, strikes and the cost of covering pay rises, the extra demand caused by this summer’s heatwaves, and the introduction of electronic health records. Privately they accuse NHS England of forcing them to adopt unreasonable savings targets in order to help the health service as a whole balance its books, because hospitals have been told to stop overspending.

In an illustration of the impact that savings drives can have, in August people in Kent with cancer had to wait up to a month for appointments before they could start chemotherapy; this was because the cancer unit had fewer nurses on duty than usual after the East Kent trust cut rates of pay to work extra “bank” shifts as part of a cost-cutting plan, which led to understaffing.

The trust admitted in a paper that its board discussed it was seeing “increasing waits for new patient appointments and pre-chemo appointments … due to lack of take-up of bank shifts due to [pay] rate changes”.

In September, York and Scarborough trust said it would shut a 28-bed ward at Bridlington community hospital, a “step-down” facility that looks after people recently discharged from hospital before they go home, to help it save £1m. It did so despite the risk this will add to pressures on beds at its two acute hospitals.

The trust also looked into withdrawing the maternity and radiology services it provided at Whitby community hospital as another of its “opportunities for efficiencies”, to save an estimated £200,000. However, those plans were “no longer being considered”, it said. It is also considering cutting the opening hours of the three urgent treatment centres it runs in York, Scarborough and Malton, to save a further £200,000, even though such services are intended to prevent overcrowding of A&E units. The trust refused to answer questions the Guardian asked about that.

Harrogate and district trust has decided to stop providing out-of-hours GP care in Hambleton and Richmond, covering a large swathe of rural Yorkshire, after 15 years because it can no longer afford to do so. It is unclear who will offer patients that service in the future.

Sherwood Forest trust’s plan to close a hydrotherapy pool at King’s Mill hospital in Sutton-in-Ashfield, to save £150,000-£200,000, has provoked an outcry. The pool is used to help rehabilitate about 1,500 patients a year, including those with long-term health conditions or those recovering from car crashes or a hip replacement, said the local Labour MP, Steve Yemm.

Sara Hazzard, of the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy, said: “The proposed closing of this pool is deeply concerning and risks depriving vulnerable patients of vital specialist rehabilitation. For people with chronic long-term conditions, aquatic physiotherapy is a clinical lifeline. The warmth and buoyancy of the water help people to manage pain, exercise and maintain mobility when land-based rehabilitation may not be suitable”.

Sherwood Forest also recently admitted in a paper discussed by its board that “financial restraints, including the need to reduce bank and agency spend, may lead to impacts on ability to maintain patient care and safety”.

Torbay and South Devon trust is axing 199 non-clinical posts and charging staff more for parking and food to help it meet its £54.4m “cost improvement plan” target. It has an underlying deficit of £100m.

In a paper submitted to its 5 November board meeting, it said it would “assess all available options to close the forecast risk gap and deliver financial plan, including ‘unpalatable’ and high-risk options”. NHS England has told its leaders to break even this year or risk having their performance being reviewed, which could lead to them being replaced.

The NHS is so short of cash that it cannot afford to have the number of beds it needs to help hospitals cope this winter, Emma Rowland, NHS England’s executive director for performance and recovery, told MPs earlier this month.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

One trust boss said: “I have been a [trust] chief executive for more than 10 years and the NHS’s finances are as tough as they have ever been. Many trusts are forecasting deficits larger than recent years. Balancing the books often means breakeven. Very few trusts will break even and many will miss their financial plan for this year.”

Trusts are also cutting jobs in a desperate effort to save money. For example, Nottingham university hospitals trust plans to shrink its workforce by 1,279 to help it meet its £106m savings target for 2026-27. It admits that a third of its identified savings are “high risk”.

Similarly, Barts health trust in London aims to axe 1,100 posts to save money.

Dr Tony O’Sullivan, a co-chair of the campaign group Keep Our NHS Public, said: “This financial straitjacket on the NHS is deeply irresponsible and the consequences are devastating. Years of underinvestment have left trusts being asked to make huge savings while demand and costs keep rising.

“AI can’t staff a ward, and another reorganisation won’t reopen a single bed. Closing step-down beds means some patients will spend longer in hospital waiting for somewhere safe to go. That leaves fewer beds for people waiting in A&E and makes it harder to carry out planned operations”

O’Sullivan added that Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, should ask the chancellor for emergency funding for the NHS to help it cope with the pressure it is under. The Department of Health and Social Care’s total spending for 2025-26 was £217bn, most of which went to the NHS.

NHS England did not respond directly over the widespread cost-cutting. A spokesperson said: “The NHS did an amazing job last year to bring its finances in within budget for the first time in more than a decade, while also delivering record levels of treatments and operations to patients.

“This has been another challenging year, and NHS boards are rightly being transparent about financial risks and taking action to mitigate them. Across the NHS, organisations are working hard to improve productivity, live within their means and make the best use of taxpayers’ money, while continuing to deliver the care people need.”

items.title: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
items.summary: The Army says "swift action" is necessary to protect its personnel and nearby communities around its ammunition plant in Iowa.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByRebecka Pieder

Updated 39 minutes ago

The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."

The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.

The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.

In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.

It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".

The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.

Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.

On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.

Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.

The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".

One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.

"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing.

The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.

The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

items.title: Hakeem Jeffries willing to cross political aisle to work on Democrats’ agenda
items.summary: Incoming House speaker says party focused on affordability and fixing ‘broken’ healthcare and immigration systems The incoming US House speaker, Hakeem Jeffries , has said he and his fellow Democrats are focused on affordability, expanding healthcare and fixing the “broken” immigration system in the…
items.body:
Hakeem Jeffries, who was nominated by Democrats as House speaker, laid out agenda in an interview on Sunday. Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/Shutterstock

Hakeem Jeffries, who was nominated by Democrats as House speaker, laid out agenda in an interview on Sunday. Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/Shutterstock

Hakeem Jeffries willing to cross political aisle to work on Democrats’ agenda

Incoming House speaker says party focused on affordability and fixing ‘broken’ healthcare and immigration systems

The incoming US House speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, has said he and his fellow Democrats are focused on affordability, expanding healthcare and fixing the “broken” immigration system in the country – and willing to cross the political aisle to do so.

Jeffries laid out that agenda in an interview on Sunday with CBS News’s Face the Nation, less than three weeks after Democrats seized control of Congress during the 3 November midterms for the latter half of Donald Trump’s second presidency.

“We need to drive down the high cost of living and deal with the affordability crisis,” the New York representative told Face the Nation host Margaret Brennan.

“We have a broken healthcare system. We need to fix it, and then make sure that we actually don’t simply return to the status quo, but we do much better than what currently exists. And we need to fix our broken immigration system as well.”

Trump’s Republican party resoundingly lost the midterms amid dissatisfaction with both high living costs worsened by the Iran war as well as his aggressive but unpopular mass deportation campaign.

Jeffries said those areas were among the ones to possibly “explore whether we can work together with the president and our colleagues on the other side of the aisle”.

He told Brennan that he envisions Democrats and Republicans working together particularly on a bipartisan healthcare plan.

Additionally, Jeffries reiterated his support for legislation banning members of Congress from trading stock, referring to it as an anti-corruption measure.

“No one is going to get a pass because there’s a cost to corruption that adversely [affects] everyday Americans,” Jeffries said. “And we should begin by dealing with our own House.”

Those remarks from Jeffries came four days after Democrats nominated him as House speaker when the new Congress is sworn in. That nomination put him in line to become the first Black lawmaker to lead the US House beginning in early January.

The midterms’ outcome have given Democrats power to conduct tough oversight of Trump for the final two years of his presidency – after his Republican party had controlled Congress since the second half of Joe Biden’s Oval Office term. But Jeffries said that Democratic lawmakers were also compelled to meet more practical everyday needs for Americans.

“Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if over the next two years, we fail to do anything about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration?” Jeffries asked.

“We’re committed to bringing about the type of dramatic change the American people are demanding.”

items.title: COP31 fails to reach major climate deal as talks expose deep divisions
items.summary: The talks fail to make a breakthrough on tackling climate change after a row about mentioning fossil fuels.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

ByMark Poynting, Esme Stallard and Justin Rowlatt

BBC Climate and Science

Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.

Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.

But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.

UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".

After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".

"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.

Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.

A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.

Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.

Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".

Figure caption,

What’s next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?

Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.

Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.

But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.

"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.

The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".

"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".

Climate talks in an age of 'overshoot'

While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.

Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.

He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.

The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.

And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.

In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.

The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.

Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.

But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.

Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.

The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035

But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.

The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.

"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" today.

The UN climate process has "suffered setback before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

items.body:
Laura Gallacher: ‘I will continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family.’ Photograph: Jack Taylor/Reuters

Laura Gallacher: ‘I will continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family.’ Photograph: Jack Taylor/Reuters

Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy

Laura Gallacher says in new video on YouTube she will continue Sunday Service series she started with Brand

Laura Gallacher, Russell Brand’s wife, has promised to “absolutely honour” rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on Sunday.

This week Andy Burnham called on Google to take down a video uploaded to Brand’s YouTube channel last Sunday that contained a statement from the disgraced comedian in prison, where he is serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults.

Gallacher began the latest episode of Sunday Service – described as a Christian series, which the couple started together six months ago – by telling viewers: “Last week’s episode drew considerable amount of attention and now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that.”

She went on to address scrutiny regarding her continuing to run her husband’s YouTube channel, amid a Ministry of Justice inquiry focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.

“I am choosing to continue Sunday Service because I really enjoy it,” Gallacher said. “It is also a place where I will continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media’s image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny.”

In the previous episode, the first published since Brand was jailed – after being convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November – Gallacher read out a message from him protesting that he was not guilty.

The video, titled “The Good Work Continues”, has remained on YouTube despite ministers repeatedly asking for it to be removed.

That video has now accumulated more than 1m views, becoming the best-performing video on Brand’s channel since 5 December last year, when he published a video conversation he had with the American conservative influencer Candace Owens. Many of his videos in the last year have drawn only between 50,000 and 100,000 views.

On Thursday night, Burnham said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down such content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. You know, why are we having to hear from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”

On Thursday night, Burnham said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down such content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. You know, why are we having to hear from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”
